titre: Beowulf Did Not Vanish in 1731; It Crumbled Afterward
accroche: Beowulf's unique manuscript survived the fire of 1731, but its margins kept falling away: about 2,000 letters survive only in copies.
contenu_vulgarise:
A single manuscript has transmitted *Beowulf*, the most famous poem in Old English. Without it, the text would not exist. It is often said that it nearly vanished in a fire in 1731. That is accurate, but it is only the beginning of the story: the fire marked the parchment, and the losses of text came mostly afterward.

## A Night in October

The manuscript belonged to the collection of Sir Robert Cotton, housed at Ashburnham House, in Westminster. On October 23, 1731, a fire breaks out there. The volume that contains *Beowulf*, bound under the shelfmark Cotton Vitellius A xv, is hit, but not destroyed.

The first accounts exaggerate. The *Dictionary of National Biography* notes that reports of the damage were “exaggerated,” and a 1732 report counts 746 volumes intact out of 958. Other manuscripts were less lucky: the unique copy of *The Battle of Maldon*, another poem in Old English, burned entirely.

## The Losses Come After

The edges of the *Beowulf* leaves are scorched. There is no serious restoration attempt before the 19th century: an effective repair is applied only in 1842, under the direction of Frederick Madden. In the meantime, the burned margins crumbled and letters fell away.

We know how many because copies exist. Between 1787 and 1790, the Icelandic scholar Grímur Jónsson Thorkelin has two transcriptions of the manuscript made: the first, in all likelihood by James Matthews, the second in his own hand. These two transcriptions preserve about 2,000 letters that the manuscript has since lost. Humphrey Wanley, who had described the poem in 1705, even preserves six of them, predating the fire.

## The Shift

The conservation work itself hid letters that the fire had spared. For Kevin Kiernan's electronic edition, illumination by transmitted light made more than 1,300 letters and fragments of letters reappear, masked by the conservation work, and ultraviolet light revealed more than a hundred erased or faded readings.

The *Beowulf* we read today therefore rests on several states of the same parchment: that of 1705, that of the 1780s, and that of Kiernan's electronic edition, reread by transmitted light and under ultraviolet light. How many of today's legible letters will no longer be so in two centuries, for lack of a new copy?

quiz.question: Why are the copies made for Thorkelin between 1787 and 1790 valuable?
choix: They reproduce a second manuscript of the poem, kept at the Royal Library in Copenhagen
They were made before the fire of 1731 and measure its damage
They correct the errors of medieval scribes that the manuscript preserved
They preserve about 2,000 letters, since lost in the manuscript
quiz.explication: The Beowulf manuscript is unique, and Thorkelin's copies reproduce it. They date from more than half a century after the fire of 1731, but from before part of the crumbling of the scorched margins: they therefore preserve letters the parchment lost afterward. No second manuscript exists, they do not predate the fire, and they are not scribal corrections.

choix: The manuscript of The Battle of Maldon
The catalog of the Cotton library
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The text explicitly contrasts Beowulf, only damaged, with the unique copy of The Battle of Maldon, which burned entirely in the same fire.

quiz_supplementaire.question: When is an effective repair of Beowulf's burned margins finally applied?
choix: As early as 1731, immediately after the fire
In 1842, under the direction of Frederick Madden
In 1900, during the transfer to the British Library
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The text specifies that there is no serious attempt before the nineteenth century and that an effective repair is applied only in 1842, under Madden; the attempt of 1824 was not enough.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What did the transmitted-light illumination used for Kevin Kiernan's electronic edition reveal?
choix: The name of the medieval scribe who copied the manuscript
The exact date of the poem's original composition
A complete second copy hidden beneath the leaves
More than 1,300 letters masked by the conservation work
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The entry states that transmitted-light illumination made more than 1,300 letters and letter fragments, masked by the conservation work, reappear, and not a date or a scribe's name.
